claims.text: Corrosion protection in as-received Q235 steel is controlled by the nature of the oxide scale that forms.
At room temperature, Q235 steel develops a thin, adherent iron oxide layer.
The room-temperature iron oxide layer slows further degradation of Q235 steel.
At 700–900 °C, aggressive salts cause fluxing reactions that transform the oxide layer into a porous, non-adherent scale.
Formation of a porous, non-adherent scale accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a low-carbon, low-alloy microstructure containing typical inclusions and impurities.
Oxide thickness, porosity, continuity, and adherence mediate whether the surface remains protective.
Limited room-temperature oxidation promotes a continuous and adherent oxide layer.
High-temperature salt exposure destabilizes the oxide and makes it prone to spallation.
Scale spallation exposes the underlying metal and thereby produces rapid degradation.
Room-temperature samples will exhibit minimal mass change, a thin adherent oxide, and limited spallation.
High-temperature salt-exposed samples will have greater mass change than high-temperature salt-free controls.
High-temperature salt-exposed samples will develop thicker, more porous, cracked, and spalled scales than high-temperature salt-free controls.
High-temperature salt-exposed samples will undergo accelerated substrate corrosion relative to high-temperature salt-free controls.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply specifically to low-carbon, as-received Q235 steel.
The mechanism may not apply to alloyed or stainless steels because Cr, Ni, and other alloying elements alter oxide formation and corrosion resistance.
Surface inclusions and minor compositional heterogeneities may affect the temperature or kinetics of the transition from protective to nonprotective oxide.
Comparable protection or mass change between salt-exposed and salt-free high-temperature samples would falsify the proposed salt-fluxing mechanism.
